inequality-s3.title: Changes on the island of Corrin
inequality-s3.text: On the invented island of Corrin: (1) workers with technical training see their wages rise much faster than other workers' wages; (2) the island starts sending monthly payments to households with very low incomes; (3) a few families pass large fortunes to their children, who earn income from the land and businesses they inherit.

items.q: Label the axes and both curves of a graph used to show how income is shared among households.

why.correct: The horizontal axis is the cumulative percentage of households, from the poorest; the vertical axis is the cumulative percentage of income they hold. The straight diagonal is the line of equality, and the curve bowed below it is the Lorenz curve.

items.q: A new program gives cash payments to the lowest-income households, paid for by taxes on higher incomes. Shift the Lorenz curve to show the change in the distribution of income after taxes and payments.

why.correct: The poorest households now hold a larger share of income, so the Lorenz curve moves toward the line of equality (up, closer to the diagonal).

key.because: cash payments to low-income households paid for by taxes on higher incomes

slips.LC: Moving the curve further from the diagonal would show more inequality; payments to the lowest-income households make the shares more equal.

items.q: Over a decade, the richest fifth of households in an invented country gains a much larger share of income while the other fifths' shares shrink. Shift the Lorenz curve to show the change.

why.correct: Income becomes less equally shared, so the Lorenz curve bows further away from the line of equality (down).

key.because: a larger income share for the richest fifth

items.q: The Gini coefficient compares one area of this graph with the whole triangle under the line of equality. Shade that area.

why.correct: The Gini coefficient is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve (region gini), taken as a share of the whole triangle under the line. The bigger that area, the more unequal the distribution.

slips.below: That is the area under the Lorenz curve. The Gini coefficient uses the gap between the line of equality and the curve.

items.q: Use the table. What cumulative percentage of income do the lowest 60 percent of households hold? This is the height of Velmora's Lorenz curve at 60 percent of households.

why.correct: Add the three lowest fifths: 3 + 8 + 15 = 26 percent.

mistakes.why: 15 percent is the middle fifth alone. A Lorenz curve is cumulative: add the lowest three fifths.
60 percent is where the line of equality would be. Velmora's households hold less: 3 + 8 + 15.

items.q: Use the table. At 40 percent of households, how far below the line of equality is Velmora's Lorenz curve?
options: 32 percentage points: 40 against 8
0 points: the curve meets the line there
29 points: 40 on the line, 11 on the curve
15 percentage points: 40 against 25

why.correct: On the line of equality each 20 percent of households holds 20 percent of income. The gap shows how much less the lower groups hold.
options: 8 is the second fifth alone; the curve is cumulative, 3 + 8 = 11.
The curve meets the line only at 0 and 100 percent here.
Right: the lowest two fifths hold 3 + 8 = 11 percent, against 40 percent with equal shares.
The lowest two fifths hold 11 percent, not 25.

items.q: Use the table. Which fifths of households receive more than an equal share of income? Select all that apply.
options: Lowest fifth
Second fifth
Middle fifth
Fourth fifth
Highest fifth

why.correct: With equal shares, each fifth would get 20 percent.
options: 3 percent is below 20.
8 percent is below 20.
15 percent is below 20.
Right: 24 percent is above 20.
Right: 50 percent is above 20.

items.q: Use the table. A neighboring country's lowest 60 percent of households hold 35 percent of income. Compared with Velmora, its Lorenz curve at 60 percent of households is
options: closer to the line of equality, so income there is more equally shared
further from the line of equality, so income there is less equally shared
on the line of equality
the same distance from the line, since both countries have five fifths

why.correct: The closer the Lorenz curve is to the diagonal, the more equal the distribution.
options: Right: 35 percent is nearer the 60 percent equal-share point than Velmora's 26.
A higher cumulative share at the same point means the curve is higher, nearer the diagonal.
Equal shares would give 60 percent.
The groups are the same size; their shares differ.

items.q: Use the table. Under Plan B, what percentage of its income does the \$100,000 household pay in tax?

why.correct: Average tax rate = tax ÷ income × 100 = \$4,000 ÷ \$100,000 × 100 = 4 percent.

mistakes.why: 10 percent is the \$20,000 household's rate. Use the \$100,000 row.
5 percent is Plan A's rate for that household. Use the Plan B column.

items.q: Use the table. What kind of tax is Plan A?
options: Progressive: higher incomes pay more dollars of tax
Regressive: lower incomes pay a larger share
Lump-sum: each household pays a fixed amount
Proportional: every household pays 5 percent of its income

why.correct: Classify a tax by the share of income it takes (the average tax rate), not by the dollar amount.
options: Paying more dollars is not enough; the share of income must rise with income.
Each household pays the same 5 percent.
The amounts differ by income.

items.q: Use the table. What kind of tax is Plan B?
options: Progressive: the \$100,000 household pays the most dollars
Regressive: its share of income falls as income rises
Proportional: each household pays some tax
Progressive: the share of income rises with income

why.correct: Regressive taxes take a larger share of lower incomes.
options: It pays more dollars but a smaller share of its income.
Right: 10 percent, then 6, then 4.
Proportional means the same share of income for all.
The share falls from 10 percent to 4 percent.

items.q: In the scenario, which change is a transfer payment?
options: (1) faster wage growth for trained workers
(2) monthly payments to low-income households
(3) inherited land and businesses
(1) and (3) together, since both change income

why.correct: Transfer payments, such as cash aid to low-income households, change the distribution of income after taxes and transfers.
options: Wages are payments for labor, earned in a factor market.
Right: money paid by the government with no good or service given in return.
An inheritance passes wealth within a family; it is not a government payment.
The monthly payments are not earned.

items.q: In the scenario, how does change (1) affect Corrin's Lorenz curve, if nothing else changes?
options: It moves toward the line of equality
It does not change, because wages are not income
It becomes the line of equality
It bows further from the line of equality

why.correct: Differences in skills and training (human capital) are a major source of income inequality.
options: The gap between trained and other workers grows.
Wages are most households' main income.
That would need every household to have the same income.
Right: trained workers, already earning more, pull further ahead, so income is less equally shared.

items.q: In the scenario, change (3) is mainly an example of which difference?
options: Wealth inequality, which also earns income
A transfer payment from the government
A regressive tax on the families' inheritance
A rise in the wages of trained workers

why.correct: Income is a flow earned over a period; wealth is a stock of assets. Wealth earns income, so the two inequalities are linked.
options: Right: inherited assets are wealth, and the rent and profit they earn is income.
The fortunes pass within families.
Nothing in (3) is a tax, and inheriting is not taxed in the scenario.
That is change (1).

items.q: What does a Lorenz curve show?
options: How one household's income changes over the course of its lifetime
The tax rate paid at each level of income
Cumulative income shares held by cumulative shares of households
The number of households at each level of income

why.correct: If every household had the same income, the Lorenz curve would be the diagonal line of equality.
options: It is a snapshot across households, not over time for one household.
Tax rates are shown in a tax table; the curve shows shares of income.
Right: each point says what percent of income the lowest x percent of households hold.
That would be a bar chart of incomes, not cumulative shares.

items.q: Which statement describes a progressive tax?
options: It takes the same share of income from everyone
It takes a larger share from lower incomes
It charges each household the same dollar amount
It takes a larger share of income as income rises

why.correct: Progressive, proportional and regressive describe how the share of income taken changes as income rises.
options: That is a proportional tax.
That is a regressive tax.
That is a lump-sum tax, which is regressive as a share of income.
Right: the average tax rate rises with income.

items.q: The Gini coefficient of one invented country rises from 0.30 to 0.40. What does that mean?
options: Income became more equally distributed
Income became less equally distributed
Total income rose by 10 percent
The tax system became more progressive

why.correct: The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one household has all the income).
options: A lower Gini coefficient would mean more equality.
Right: a higher Gini coefficient means a larger area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve.
The Gini coefficient measures how income is shared, not how much there is.
That would usually lower after-tax inequality, not raise it.

items.q: Which of these are sources of income inequality? Select all that apply.
options: Differences in education and job training
Inherited wealth that earns rent, interest or profit
Each household receiving the same transfer payment
A proportional tax that takes the same share from each household
Discrimination in hiring or pay

why.correct: Income differs with skills, wealth, discrimination, market power, effort and luck.
options: Right: more human capital tends to raise wages.
Right: income from assets adds to the gap.
Equal payments lower inequality as a share of income.
It leaves income shares where they were.
Right: it lowers the earnings of the people discriminated against.

items.q: A country makes its income tax more progressive and spends the revenue on transfer payments to low-income households. What happens to the Lorenz curve for income after taxes and transfers?
options: It moves away from the line of equality
It does not move, because total income is the same
It moves toward the line of equality
It becomes the line of equality

why.correct: Progressive taxes and transfers are the main policies that move the after-tax Lorenz curve toward equality.
options: Both changes narrow the gap between high and low incomes.
The curve shows shares, and the shares change.
Right: higher incomes keep a smaller share and lower incomes gain, so shares are more equal.
Shares become more equal, not exactly equal.
